opinions.rationale: Inverted-prior search finds substantial prior art that already structures protocol-paired data fitness and can return no, so the claim that fitness is only a narrative paragraph with no thresholds and no procedure that can stop a study is overstated. SPIFD (2021) and SPIFD2 (2023) are step-by-step feasibility frameworks that pair research question, target-trial articulation, and data-source selection, with component-level documentation and heatmaps intended to support go or no-go decisions before estimation. The CARE oncology work (Levy et al., 2026) runs a systematic multi-stage fitness screen over six commercial EHR sources and 23 candidate RCTs: of 54 RCT-RWD combinations, nine reached detailed feasibility and only three were selected for emulation protocol development, with explicit fitness constraints (complex eligibility, biomarkers, performance status, outcome ascertainment). OHDSI DataQualityDashboard implements quantitative pass/fail thresholds on CDM conformance, and DARWIN EU study phases include a feasibility assessment that issues a recommendation on whether to conduct the study. Lee et al. (2026) quantifies TTE-relevant completeness, accuracy, plausibility, and concordance for an EHR cohort against Medicare claims, and Wang et al. (2026) formalizes when EHR realization of trial components can or cannot yield interpretable estimates. What remains open is exactly the hard part of the proposed agenda: field-standard, protocol-component fitness scores with pre-specified stop rules that academic pipelines cannot bypass; routine publication of negative fitness assessments as citable results; and empirical validation that low fitness predicts poor concordance with the corresponding trial. Regulatory and industry pathways already gate more often than the report implies; general-purpose TTE software (TrialEmulation and related packages) still does not enforce a fitness gate that returns no.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: Outside tightly gated regulatory or network feasibility processes, many published target trial emulations still assert data suitability narratively, and there is no field-standard, protocol-component fitness score with pre-specified stop rules that is routinely published when it fails and has been validated against trial concordance.

opinions.rationale: The report's own cited work, Li et al. (FL-TTE, 2025), demonstrates that distributed effect estimation for an emulated trial is feasible without pooling patient-level data. That is estimation machinery, not a solution to semantic incompatibility: sites can still implement different eligibility, exposure, or outcome mappings under the same executable protocol, and averaging site estimates does not detect that. Manke-Reimers et al. (2025) is a scoping review of transportability practice; it clarifies when a multi-site average needs an explicit transport model, but does not supply site-level diagnostics that separate mapping failure from true effect modification using only the aggregates federation is allowed to share. Recent federated causal-inference methods (for example Khellaf, Bellet, and Josse on propensity-score aggregation across sites; LATTE one-shot federated TTE showcased at OHDSI 2025) again address statistical pooling and privacy-preserving nuisance estimation, not semantic trial equivalence. Queries across AJE/Epidemiology/IJE/EJE/PDS/SiM, arXiv stat.ME, medRxiv, and package ecosystems (TrialEmulation, lmtp, ltmle, WeightIt, MatchIt, gfoRmula) did not surface a released method that gates secure aggregation behind site-level trial-component validation or that diagnoses coding-system and phenotype discordance from sufficient statistics and aggregate balance alone. Heterogeneity statistics remain confounded between real effect modification and mapping failure, exactly as the problem states. Status remains open as stated.

The core claim is still true and was not overturned by 2024-2026 literature or software: common data models (OMOP and peers) standardize structure and vocabulary mapping, but do not guarantee semantic or causal equivalence of analytic variables across sites or years, and the mapping history and extract versions needed to check drift are still rarely published with target trial emulations. TARGET (2025) improves reporting of how the trial protocol is mapped to observational data, and OHDSI tools (DataQualityDashboard, CohortDiagnostics, standardized vocabularies) improve structural quality and phenotype characterization, but neither certifies that the same column means the same clinical construct. Work that partially implements pieces of the proposed direction exists and should not be ignored: Guha and Reiter (2024) fuse Bayesian probabilistic record linkage with causal estimators so linkage uncertainty propagates into treatment-effect inference rather than being collapsed to a hard match (bipartite two-file setting, evaluated in simulation and survey data, not multi-source claims-EHR-registry TTE as standard practice); Johns, Baum, and Prasser (2025) track provenance through clinical-warehouse ETL for quality management; semi-automated linkage provenance prototypes appear in the data-linkage literature. Those are proposals or infrastructure for components of the agenda, not a solved provenance-plus-invariance-plus-leave-one-source-out standard for multi-source TTE. The BMJ 2025 concordance review supports that design and outcome emulation quality matter for trial agreement, which makes provenance consequential, but does not itself close the semantic-equivalence gap. Searches for phenotype temporal-drift diagnostics, published source-to-analytic provenance graphs in TTE, and routine leave-one-source-out multi-source analyses as standard practice returned methods papers and tools, not field resolution. Vote open; partial methods noted in rationale without over-crediting them as solutions.
